planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; this patented dwarf selection is propagated only by division or cuttings, not seed.

directions: This compact, congested-flowering sport of great blue lobelia was bred and patented by Terra Nova Nurseries from open-pollinated dwarf siphilitica lines. It forms a tight basal clump of strong, short flowering stems topped with dense spikes of white, two-lipped flowers in mid to late summer, standing noticeably shorter than the typical species and holding up well without staking. Give it the same wet-footed conditions great blue lobelia demands in the wild: a pond margin, rain garden, or consistently moist border bed in partial shade. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and flower density.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP15,095 (Terra Nova Nurseries)

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; like its sister selection 'White Candles', this cultivar is propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.

directions: A sister selection to 'White Candles' from the same Terra Nova Nurseries breeding line, this cultivar keeps the dwarf habit and congested flowering stems but reverts to a soft lilac-blue bloom color closer to the species' natural palette, just richer and more floriferous. The short, sturdy stems resist flopping better than wild-type great blue lobelia and carry densely packed spikes from midsummer into fall. Plant it where soil stays reliably moist to wet, such as a bog garden or stream-bank planting, in partial shade for best flower color and stem strength. Lift and divide crowded clumps every several years to keep plants vigorous.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP15,236 (Terra Nova Nurseries)

planting.note: Transplant rooted sprigs or small divisions into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade during spring so the mat has a full growing season to knit together before winter.

directions: A selected named form of the native evergreen groundcover partridgeberry, chosen for an especially low, dense mat barely rising off the soil surface, even flatter than typical wild plants. It carries the species' small paired glossy leaves, tiny fused white summer flowers, and bright red winter berries, but knits together into a tighter carpet that suits small-scale woodland and terrarium plantings. Grow it exactly as you would the species: deep shade, constant moisture, and strongly acidic, humus-rich soil, ideally worked in among pine bark or leaf litter under broadleaf evergreens. Top-dress with leaf mold annually rather than disturbing the shallow, mat-forming roots.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
